{{confusing|date=September 2008}}

In [[statistics]], the '''Khmaladze transformation''' is a mathematical tool used in constructing convenient [[goodness of fit]] tests for hypothetical [[Cumulative distribution function|distribution functions]]. More precisely, suppose <math>X_1,\ldots, X_n</math> are [[i.i.d.]], possibly multi-dimensional, random observations generated from an unknown [[probability distribution]]. A classical problem in statistics is to decide how well a given hypothetical distribution function <math>F</math>, or a given hypothetical parametric family of distribution functions <math> \{ F_\theta : \theta \in \Theta \}</math>, fits the set of observations. The Khmaladze transformation allows us to construct goodness of fit tests with desirable properties. It is named after [[Estate V. Khmaladze]].

Consider the sequence of [[empirical distribution function]]s <math>F_n</math> based on a sequence of i.i.d random variables, <math>X_1,\ldots, X_n</math>, as ''n'' increases. Suppose <math>F</math> is the hypothetical [[Cumulative distribution function|distribution function]] of each <math>X_i</math>. To test whether the choice of <math>F</math> is correct or not, statisticians use the normalized difference,

: <math>v_n(x)=\sqrt{n} [F_n(x)-F(x)].</math>

This <math>v_n</math>, as a [[Stochastic process|random process]] in <math>x</math>, is called the [[empirical process]]. Various [[Functional (mathematics)|functional]]s of <math>v_n</math> are used as test statistics. The change of the variable <math>v_n(x)=u_n(t)</math>, <math>t=F(x)</math> transforms to the so-called uniform empirical process <math>u_n</math>. The latter is an empirical processes based on independent random variables <math>U_i=F(X_i)</math>, which are [[uniform distribution (continuous)|uniformly distributed]] on <math>[0,1]</math> if the <math>X_i</math>s do indeed have distribution function <math>F</math>.

This fact was discovered and first utilized by Kolmogorov (1933), Wald and Wolfowitz (1936) and Smirnov (1937) and, especially after Doob (1949) and Anderson and Darling (1952),<ref>{{cite journal |title=Asymptotic Theory of Certain "Goodness of Fit" Criteria Based on Stochastic Processes |first=T. W. |last=Anderson |first2=D. A. |last2=Darling |journal=[[Annals of Mathematical Statistics]] |volume=23 |issue=2 |year=1952 |pages=193–212 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177729437 |doi-access=free }}</ref> it led to the standard rule to choose test statistics based on <math>v_n</math>. That is, test statistics <math>\psi(v_n,F)</math> are defined (which possibly depend on the <math>F</math> being tested) in such a way that there exists another statistic <math>\varphi(u_n)</math> derived from the uniform empirical process, such that <math>\psi(v_n,F)=\varphi(u_n)</math>. Examples are

: <math>\sup_x|v_n(x)|=\sup_t|u_n(t)|,\quad \sup_x\frac{|v_n(x)|}{a(F(x))}=\sup_t\frac {|u_n(t)|}{a(t)}</math>

and

: <math>\int_{-\infty}^\infty v_n^2(x) \, dF(x)=\int_0^1 u_n^2(t)\,dt.</math>

For all such functionals, their [[null distribution]] (under the hypothetical <math>F</math>) does not depend on <math>F</math>, and can be calculated once and then used to test any <math>F</math>.

However, it is only rarely that one needs to test a simple hypothesis, when a fixed <math>F</math> as a hypothesis is given. Much more often, one needs to verify parametric hypotheses where the  hypothetical <math>F=F_{\theta_n}</math>, depends on some parameters <math>\theta_n</math>, which the hypothesis does not specify and which have to be estimated from the sample <math>X_1,\ldots,X_n</math> itself.

Although the estimators <math>\hat \theta_n</math>, most commonly converge to true value of <math>\theta</math>, it was discovered that the parametric,<ref name="Kac, Kiefer and Wolfowitz 1955">{{cite journal |title=On Tests of Normality and Other Tests of Goodness of Fit Based on Distance Methods |first=M. |last=Kac |first2=J. |last2=Kiefer |first3=J. |last3=Wolfowitz |journal=[[Annals of Mathematical Statistics]] |volume=26 |issue=2 |year=1955 |pages=189–211 |jstor=2236876 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177728538|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Gikhman 1954">Gikhman (1954){{full citation needed|date=August 2013}}</ref> or estimated, empirical process

: <math>\hat v_n(x)=\sqrt{n} [F_n(x)-F_{\hat\theta_n}(x)]</math>

differs significantly from <math>v_n</math> and that the transformed process <math>\hat u_n(t)=\hat v_n(x)</math>, <math>t=F_{\hat\theta_n}(x)</math> has a distribution for which the limit distribution, as <math>n\to\infty</math>, is dependent on the parametric form of <math>F_{\theta}</math> and on the particular estimator <math>\hat\theta_n</math> and, in general, within one [[parametric family]], on the value of <math>\theta</math>.

From mid-1950s to the late-1980s, much work was done to clarify the situation and understand the nature of the process <math>\hat v_n</math>.

In 1981,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Khmaladze |first=E. V. |year=1981 |title=Martingale Approach in the Theory of Goodness-of-fit Tests |journal= Theory of Probability & Its Applications|volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=240–257 |doi=10.1137/1126027 }}</ref> and then 1987 and 1993,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Khmaladze |first=E. V. |year=1993 |title=Goodness of fit Problems and Scanning Innovation Martingales |journal=[[Annals of Statistics]] |volume=21 |issue=2 |pages=798–829 |jstor=2242262 |doi=10.1214/aos/1176349152|doi-access=free }}</ref> Khmaladze suggested to replace the parametric empirical process <math>\hat v_n</math> by its martingale part <math>w_n</math> only.

: <math>\hat v_n(x)-K_n(x)=w_n(x)</math>

where <math>K_n(x)</math> is the compensator of <math>\hat v_n(x)</math>. Then the following properties of <math>w_n</math> were established:

* Although the form of <math>K_n</math>, and therefore, of <math>w_n</math>, depends on <math>F_{\hat\theta_n}(x)</math>, as a function of both <math>x</math> and <math>\theta_n</math>, the limit distribution of the time transformed process

:: <math>\omega_n(t)=w_n(x), t=F_{\hat \theta_n}(x)</math>

: is that of standard [[Brownian motion]] on <math>[0,1]</math>, i.e., is again standard and independent of the choice of <math>F_{\hat\theta_n}</math>.

* The relationship between <math>\hat v_n</math> and <math>w_n</math> and between their limits, is one to one, so that the statistical inference based on <math>\hat v_n</math> or on <math>w_n</math> are equivalent, and in <math>w_n</math>, nothing is lost compared to <math>\hat v_n</math>.
* The construction of innovation martingale <math>w_n</math> could be carried over to the case of vector-valued <math>X_1,\ldots,X_n</math>, giving rise to the definition of the so-called scanning martingales in <math>\mathbb R^d</math>.

For a long time the transformation was, although known, still not used. Later, the work of researchers like [[Roger Koenker|Koenker]], [[Winfried Stute|Stute]], [[Jushan Bai|Bai]], [[Hira L. Koul|Koul]], Koening, and others made it popular in [[econometrics]] and other fields of statistics.{{citation needed|date=August 2013}}
